appearance.organs.flower.form.flower.cup.why: A cactus's tepals are free, on a spiral that runs from the spreading outer ones to the upright inner ones about this mean rise: flat in a wheel, a bowl in a cup, a bell, a funnel, a narrow tube, a flat limb on a tube, an urn.

appearance.organs.*.shape.tube.why: A cactus's tepals stand on the rim of a floral tube, the hypanthium grown up round the ovary: barely any in a wheel or a cup, as Opuntia's flowers have none above the pericarpel, short in a bell, longer in a funnel, longest in a tube or under a salver's limb; in flower radii.

appearance.organs.*.shape.petal_width.why: A cactus's inner tepals are broad and overlap at their bases in a wheel or a cup, a little narrower in a bell or a funnel, and narrow in a tube.

appearance.organs.*.shape.pericarpel.why: A cactus's ovary is sunk in its stem tissue, the pericarpel, which wears on the flower and on the bud below the closed tepals what it will wear as a fruit: nothing on a pincushion's, broad scales on a barrel's or the saguaro's, felted areoles on a prickly pear's, spiny areoles on a hedgehog's (Anderson, The Cactus Family pp. 27 to 33, 139, 231, 328 and 486).

appearance.organs.*.shape.kind.why: A cactus's fruit is its pericarpel grown on, crowned by the dried perianth: naked in a pincushion's, under broad scales in a barrel's or the saguaro's, studded with felted areoles in a prickly pear's, and with spines on those areoles in a hedgehog's, the organ pipe's or a spiny cholla's (Anderson, The Cactus Family pp. 31 to 33).

generator.params.bud_size.why: A cactus's bud is its flower closed, its pericarpel and floral tube already near their full size and its tepals swelling to open: drawn seven tenths of the open flower's width.

generator.params.bud_share.why: A cactus whose months are stated flowers in them: every place in its ring of flowers is a bud before it opens, a flower in its months and fruit after them, so none is drawn as a bud all year.

generator.params.fruit_share.why: Nor is any place drawn as fruit all year: this year's flowers become its fruit, and older fruit hang below them in older rings or chains where the species keeps them.

appearance.bodies.stem.dome.why: A cactus stem closes over as many of its tip's radii as its tip's shape says: over a length and a half where it tapers to its apex, a half sphere where it is rounded, and a short shoulder under a broad top.

appearance.bodies.stem.shoulder.why: A tapering tip narrows steadily toward its apex, a rounded one follows a quarter circle, and a broad one keeps its width into a full shoulder before turning in under its flattish top.

generator.params.dome.why: The program sets the crown's ring of flowers on the shoulder of the dome the body draws, so it takes the same length.

generator.params.fill.why: A column's old pieces, laid down narrow while the plant was young, fill out toward a share of the adult width: nearly all of it on a cylindrical stem, three quarters on a club-shaped one, which stays narrower at its foot than above (Gibson and Nobel, The Cactus Primer p. 79: a stem that elongates faster than it widens becomes club-shaped).

appearance.bodies.stem.tubercles.height.why: A tubercle stands from the stem as far as a flora's word for it says, as a share of the stem's radius: barely a swelling under each areole of a ribbed barrel (Anderson's Ferocactus wislizeni), low knobs along undulate ribs (F. cylindraceus), distinct knobs, or the prominent ones a cholla's joint is knobbly with.

appearance.bodies.stem.tubercles.stretch.why: A tubercle is as long along the stem, for its width, as its shape says: an ovoid one a little longer, an elongate one two to three times, a broadly oval one half as long again.

appearance.bodies.stem.tubercles.point.why: A conical tubercle comes to a point, a cylindrical one stands steep-sided, and rounded, elongate and broad ones are low mounds.

appearance.bodies.stem.spines.radial.dis.why: A joint's lower areoles carry fewer spines, or none, where its flora puts them mostly or only on the upper areoles: the share rises toward the tip, and where the lower areoles have none, the lower half of the joint is bare of spines.

appearance.bodies.stem.spines.central.di.why: The central spines keep to the upper areoles as the radials do.

appearance.bodies.stem.spines.main.dista.why: The main central keeps to the upper areoles as the other centrals do.

generator.params.flank.why: A column's flowers open in a ring round its apex, or also down its flank: near the tip and along the upper sides, on the last six years' growth, or from the upper half of a short, slow stem, on its last fifteen years'.

appearance.bodies.stem.colour.why: A cactus's skin is drawn in the colour its flora gives the stem or joints; its ribs' valleys darken it.

appearance.bodies.stem.spines.radial.col.why: The radial spines are drawn in the colour the flora gives the spines.

appearance.bodies.stem.spines.central.co.why: The central spines take the colour the flora gives them apart, else the spines' colour.

appearance.bodies.stem.spines.main.colou.why: The main central is a central spine and is coloured as they are.

appearance.bodies.stem.greying.colour.why: Old spines turn to the colour the flora gives them once grey or dark.

appearance.bodies.stem.areoles.felt.why: An areole's felt is drawn in the colour the flora gives its wool.

appearance.bodies.stem.ribs.count.why: A stem's ribs vary within the count its flora gives; the body draws more of them round a thicker stem.

appearance.bodies.stem.areoles.spacing.why: Areoles sit along a rib's crest, or over a joint, this far apart.

appearance.bodies.stem.spines.radial.cou.why: An areole bears as many radial spines as its flora counts, varying within its range.

appearance.bodies.stem.spines.radial.len.why: Floras give the longest spines; a set's spines vary a quarter either way about its length, so the longest stand about a quarter above it.

appearance.bodies.stem.spines.central.co.why: An areole bears as many central spines as its flora counts. Where one central stands apart as the main one, the others are set by hand, so the two sets together make the count.

appearance.bodies.stem.spines.central.le.why: As for the radials: the longest central stands about a quarter above the set's length.

appearance.bodies.stem.spines.main.lengt.why: The main central is the longest a flora gives, about a quarter above its set's length.

traits.flowering_position.note: Wikipedia, Cactus (read 2026-10-16): flowers arise from areoles (upper part), mostly near the growing stem tips; DELTA Cactaceae: terminal or lateral. Areoles are lateral short shoots, so lateral, clustered near the apex.

traits.stamens.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 374: stamens numerous, spiral or in clusters on the hypanthium (Floral Diagrams p. 192: arising centrifugally on a ring). Book writes ∞ (numerous); 200 is our stand-in for the upper bound and 20 for 'numerous' with no stated lower bound.

traits.carpels.note: Ronse De Craene, Floral Diagrams (2010) p. 192: carpels (3) 4 to 5, up to 18; Simpson p. 374 says 3 to many.

traits.spines.note: Britton and Rose's The Cactaceae (vol. 1, 1919, p. 8): every cactus has areoles, special organs in the axils of its leaves or where they would be, which bear its spines (and glochids, hairs or glands), its branches and its flowers.

traits.note: Abrams's Illustrated Flora of the Pacific States, volume 3 (1951), read in full (Cactaceae by I. L. Wiggins): perianth segments numerous, grading from sepals to petals, imbricated, their bases coalescent in a cup or tube borne on the apex of the ovary; stamens numerous, on the throat of the tube; ovary inferior, 1-celled; style 1, stigma lobes 1 to numerous. Jepson eFlora (as quoted in search results; the page itself was not read): flowers radial, rarely bilateral. No flora counts the tepals.

generator.program.note: The cacti's own program (growth plan G2.3a): columns, barrels and chains of joints, their ribs, areoles and spines from each species' look.

rules.note: Spec rework E6c: the cacti's ribs, areoles and spines grown from the characters their floras state, in each body look that has ribs or a spine set of that role.

traits.perianth_parts.note: Anderson, The Cactus Family (2001) pp. 19 and 33: the perianth is many segments grading from scale bracts through sepal-like to petal-like tepals; Kubitzki vol. 5 (2003) p. 13: spiral, partly acyclic, the parts indeterminate in number; Gibson and Nobel, The Cactus Primer p. 246: many free perianth parts arranged helically. No source counts them for the family: 15 to 60, typically 30, by hand from those words, where species and genera say no more.

traits.life_span.note: Watson and Dallwitz, The Families of Flowering Plants (DELTA data, items edited May 2026), family Cactaceae: the herbs' life form (character 21), coded perennial. Read from the coded states by script (spec-rework/b1/delta/mapdelta.py with character 21 added); states the authors do not qualify, side by side, read as often.

traits.phyllotaxis_pattern.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 374, 375, 376, family Cactaceae: phyllotaxis pattern spiral; read as "spiral".

traits.leaf_division.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 374, 375, 376, family Cactaceae: leaf division simple; read as "simple".

traits.inflorescence.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 374, 375, 376, family Cactaceae: inflorescence solitary flowers in the axils (rarely terminal cymes), usually; read as {"solitary": "usually"}.

traits.sexual_system.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 374, 375, 376, family Cactaceae: sexual system hermaphrodite (rarely unisexual), usually; read as {"hermaphrodite": "usually"}.

traits.fruit_type.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 374, 375, 376, family Cactaceae: fruit type berry (rarely dry and indehiscent), usually; read as {"berry": "usually"}.
